analogy.p: An embedded system is like a bottle opener: it is small, cheap, reliable and does one job really well. A general purpose computer is like a Swiss army knife: it can do many things, but it is bigger, costs more and is not the best at any single job. The analogy breaks down because a bottle opener has no brain: an embedded system takes inputs, makes decisions and controls outputs, and it can follow a program.
analogy.t: A specialist tool versus a Swiss army knife

bullets: Know the **purpose** of an embedded system.
Know its main **characteristics**.
Be able to give **examples** of embedded systems in everyday devices.
Be able to **compare** embedded systems with general purpose computers.
Know that embedded systems sit inside a **larger device**.
Be able to explain why a device **needs** an embedded system.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: OCR J277 section 1.1 expects you to know the purpose and characteristics of embedded systems and to give examples of them. An embedded system is a computer system, usually a small processor with memory and input and output connections, built into a larger device to control one particular function. You will be asked to describe what makes a system embedded, to say how it differs from a general purpose computer such as a laptop, and to identify or explain examples such as domestic appliances or vehicle systems.

bullets: Embedded system = **computer system built into a larger device** to do a **dedicated function**.
Usually based on a **microcontroller** (CPU, memory and input/output on one chip).
The user normally **does not see** or use it as a computer.
It controls the device by receiving **input**, **processing** it and sending **output**.
It is part of the product and is designed **with** it, not added afterwards.
Contrast: a laptop is a **general purpose** computer that can run many different programs.
core.p: An embedded system is a computer system that is built into another device to carry out a specific, dedicated function. It normally contains a microprocessor or microcontroller, a small amount of memory and input and output connections to sensors and other components. It is called embedded because it is part of the device and is not usually seen or used as a computer by the person using the device. The washing machine owner simply presses a button; the embedded system inside does all of the controlling.

bullets: Purpose: **control a specific function** of a device.
Takes **inputs** from sensors, buttons or switches.
**Processes** them following a fixed program.
Sends **outputs** to motors, heaters, displays, speakers or lamps.
Allows devices to work **automatically**, accurately and consistently.
Often makes the device **safer** and more **energy efficient**.
core.p: The purpose of an embedded system is to control some or all of the functions of the device it is inside, automatically and reliably. It does this by reading information from sensors or buttons, processing it according to a stored program and then controlling outputs such as motors, heaters, lights or displays. This makes the device easier to use, more accurate and often more efficient, because the embedded system makes decisions without human help.

bullets: Designed for **one specific task** or a fixed small set of tasks.
The program is **fixed** and stored in ROM or flash memory, called **firmware**.
The user **cannot install** new software as on a computer.
The hardware is chosen to be **just powerful enough** for the job.
There is often **no keyboard, mouse or full screen**; controls are buttons or dials.
Compare: a general purpose computer can run **many different programs**.
core.p: The most important characteristic is that an embedded system does one specific job, or a small fixed set of related jobs, and nothing else. A microwave oven's controller handles timing, power and the door switch; it can never run a word processor. Because the job is known in advance, designers can use a processor and memory that are only as powerful as the task needs. The program is written for that job only and is not changed by the user.

bullets: **Low cost** to manufacture, because the hardware is simple.
**Small size**, so it can fit inside the device.
**Low power consumption**, so it can run on batteries or stay on all the time.
Simple processor, **small memory**, little or no operating system.
Often produce **little heat**, so need no big cooling.
These properties are possible **because** the task is limited.
core.h: Characteristic: small, low cost, low power
core.p: Embedded systems are usually small, cheap and use little power. They are built into products that are made in large quantities, so keeping the cost down by a few pence per unit matters a great deal. Because they only do one job they need a simple processor with little memory, which also means they are small and use far less electricity, so they can run on a battery for a long time or sit in a product permanently switched on.

bullets: Must be **reliable**, often running **for years** without failure.
Often **real-time**: respond to inputs **within a fixed short time**.
Program stored as **firmware** in **ROM / flash** (non-volatile).
**Start up instantly** when powered on, no long booting.
Fewer moving parts and a simple design make failures **less likely**.
In safety-related devices (brakes, medical) failure could be **dangerous**.
core.p: Many embedded systems must be very reliable and respond immediately, because they control things such as car brakes, pacemakers or alarms. They are often real-time systems: they must react to an input within a strict time limit. They run firmware stored in non-volatile memory, so they start working as soon as power is applied and do not lose their program when switched off. They typically run continuously for years without maintenance.

bullets: **Washing machine**: controls water level, temperature, drum speed and cycle timing.
**Microwave oven**: controls timer, power level and door safety switch.
**Central heating thermostat**: switches the boiler on and off to keep a set temperature.
**Fridge / freezer**: monitors temperature and controls the compressor.
**Dishwasher, oven, coffee machine** follow the same pattern.
All use **sensors** (input), a **small CPU** (process) and **motors / heaters** (output).
core.p: Appliances such as washing machines, microwave ovens, dishwashers, fridges and central heating thermostats contain embedded systems. In a washing machine the system reads the programme chosen, senses the water level and temperature, switches the pump, motor and heater on and off in the right order and ends the cycle when it is finished. This is why a washing machine can run unattended and gives repeatable results.

bullets: **Car engine management** (ECU): fuel injection and ignition timing.
**Anti-lock braking**, airbags, cruise control and parking sensors.
**Burglar alarms** and **smoke alarms**: read sensors and sound a siren.
**Traffic light** controllers: timed sequence of lights.
**Digital watch, smart meter, fitness tracker, TV remote**.
**Medical devices**, for example a pacemaker or an insulin pump.
core.h: Embedded systems in vehicles, security and other devices
core.p: Embedded systems are also found in vehicles, where an engine control unit (ECU) monitors sensors and controls fuel injection and ignition timing to run the engine efficiently, and other systems control anti-lock brakes, airbags and parking sensors. Security and alarm systems use embedded controllers to read door and motion sensors and trigger a siren. Other examples include traffic lights, digital watches, smart meters, MP3 players, fitness trackers, TV remote controls and medical devices such as pacemakers.

bullets: **Embedded**: one fixed task; **general purpose**: many tasks.
**Embedded**: program in ROM/flash; **general purpose**: programs loaded from storage.
**Embedded**: low cost and power; **general purpose**: higher cost and power.
**Embedded**: little or no user interface; **general purpose**: keyboard, mouse, large display.
**Embedded**: limited or no upgrade; **general purpose**: software and hardware easily upgraded.
Both have a **CPU, memory and input / output**.
core.h: Embedded systems compared with general purpose computers
core.p: A general purpose computer such as a laptop can run many different programs because it has an operating system, large memory and storage, and standard input and output devices. An embedded system is the opposite: it is built for one task, with firmware that the user does not change. This makes embedded systems cheaper, smaller and more reliable for their job, but they are inflexible and cannot easily be upgraded.

bullets: **Input**: sensors (temperature, light, motion, pressure) and buttons.
**Process**: CPU follows the firmware program.
**Output**: motors, heaters, lights, buzzers, displays.
Control programs usually **repeat in a loop** while the device is on.
Example thermostat: read temperature, if too low switch heater **on**, else switch **off**.
The loop lets the device **respond to changes** quickly and automatically.
core.h: How an embedded system works: input, process, output
core.p: Every embedded system follows the input, process, output pattern. Sensors or buttons supply input. The processor runs the firmware to decide what should happen, and then it sends output signals to actuators such as motors, heaters or lamps. In a control system this runs in a continuous loop, for example a thermostat reads the temperature, compares it with the set value, switches the heater on or off and then reads again. Because it loops repeatedly the system reacts to changes straight away.

bullets: Advantage: **low cost** and **small size**.
Advantage: **low power use**, suits batteries.
Advantage: **reliable** and quick to respond.
Advantage: **automates** a task, saving the user effort.
Disadvantage: **cannot be easily upgraded or changed**.
Disadvantage: **limited** processing power and memory.
Disadvantage: if it fails the whole device may need **replacing**.
core.p: Embedded systems have clear advantages for the devices that use them, but there are some limitations. The main advantage is that a small, cheap, low-power system can do its job very well and reliably. The main disadvantages are a lack of flexibility, difficulty of repair and upgrade, and the fact that the user cannot change what the device does. When asked to evaluate, you should give both sides in context.

bullets: Contains a **CPU** running the fetch-decode-execute cycle (1.1.2).
**ROM** holds firmware, **RAM** holds temporary data (1.2.1).
Compare with CPU **performance** factors, as embedded CPUs are often low speed (1.1.3).
Sensors and actuators link to **input and output devices**.
Internet-connected devices (smart home) link to **network security** (1.4).
**E-waste** and energy use link to environmental impact (1.6).
core.p: Embedded systems tie together several parts of Paper 1. The CPU, memory and fetch-decode-execute cycle are all there in miniature; ROM and flash relate to the storage section; and non-volatile firmware contrasts with volatile RAM. They also link to the legal and ethical topics, because devices that are always on and connected can collect data, use electricity and create e-waste when they are thrown away.

bullets: Definition mark: '**computer system** built into a **larger device** to do a **specific / dedicated task**'.
Always give a **device-specific** example from the question.
Describe **input, process, output** for the device.
For comparisons, make both sides explicit: 'embedded does one job, a laptop does many'.
For 'give an example' questions, name the **device**, not 'a computer'.
For evaluate questions, give advantages **and** disadvantages and a conclusion.
core.p: Questions often give a device and ask you to identify or justify whether it contains an embedded system. A strong answer states that it has a dedicated function, is inside a larger device and uses a small computer to control it. Do not say an embedded system is 'a small computer' on its own: you must mention that it is part of a larger device and does a specific task. Give an example drawn from the question, not a generic one.

exam: Command words: **State / Give** = short fact (1 mark); **Describe** = say what it does; **Explain** = reason with 'because'; **Discuss** = both sides with conclusion.
Definition (2 marks): 'a computer system (1) built into a larger device to perform a specific/dedicated task (1)'.
Give-an-example questions: name a **specific device** (washing machine, car engine management, thermostat, alarm).
Characteristics to quote: **dedicated function**, **small**, **low cost**, **low power**, **firmware in ROM/flash**, **reliable**.
For 'why is X an embedded system?' write: it has a **dedicated function**, is **part of a larger device**, and uses a **small computer**.
For comparison with a general purpose computer, state a feature of **each**: one task vs many; fixed program vs loaded programs.
For 3-4 mark 'describe how it works' use **input (sensor), process (CPU/firmware), output (actuator)** for the device named.
Advantage marks: low cost, small, low power, reliable. Disadvantage marks: not upgradeable, limited power, whole device replaced on failure.
Do not use the word 'smartphone' or 'laptop' as embedded examples.
Check number of marks and give that many separate points.
Use the context of the question: link every point to the **named device**.

mistakes.r: It is a computer system built into a larger device to perform a dedicated function.
mistakes.w: An embedded system is a small computer.

mistakes.r: A laptop is general purpose; an embedded system performs one specific task inside another device.
mistakes.w: A laptop is an embedded system because it has a processor.

mistakes.r: A smartphone is general purpose because it runs many apps; give a device with a single function such as a microwave or thermostat.
mistakes.w: A smartphone is a good example of an embedded system.

mistakes.r: They run fixed firmware designed for one job and the user does not normally change it.
mistakes.w: Embedded systems can run any program.

mistakes.r: It is cheap and low power because the task is simple, so the hardware only needs to be as powerful as the job requires.
mistakes.w: An embedded system is always cheap because it is slow.

mistakes.r: Name the system: for example the engine control unit controlling fuel injection and ignition timing.
Firmware is stored in non-volatile memory such as ROM or flash so it is kept when power is off.
They take input from sensors or buttons and send output to devices such as motors, heaters and displays.
mistakes.w: Embedded systems have no input or output.

summary: OCR J277 1.1 requires you to know what an embedded system is, its purpose and characteristics (dedicated function, small, low cost, low power, firmware, reliable) and to give examples such as domestic appliances, vehicle systems and security systems. It is regularly tested as 1 to 4 mark questions and as part of comparison questions.

terms.d: A computer system built into a larger device to carry out a specific, dedicated function.
A small computer on a single chip containing a processor, memory and input/output connections.
Software stored permanently in ROM or flash memory that controls the hardware of a device.
An input device that measures a physical quantity, such as temperature, light or motion.
An output device that causes a physical action, such as a motor, heater or valve.
A system that must respond to inputs within a guaranteed, very short time.
A computer designed to run many different programs, such as a laptop or desktop.
A single specific task that a device is designed to carry out.
Read only memory: non-volatile memory that stores data such as firmware and keeps it when power is off.
Non-volatile memory that can be erased and rewritten, used to store firmware.
Data or signals sent to a system, for example from a sensor or button.
Data or signals sent from a system, for example to a motor or display.
An embedded system in a vehicle that controls the engine, such as fuel injection and ignition timing.
Memory that keeps its contents when the power is turned off.

worked.ans: An embedded system is a computer system built into a larger device to do one dedicated task. Examples: the controller in a washing machine and a car's engine control unit.
worked.q: Describe what is meant by an embedded system and give two examples. [4 marks]
steps: A computer system (1) built into a larger device (1) to carry out a specific / dedicated function (1).
Examples: washing machine controller, car engine control unit, microwave, alarm (any two named devices) (1 mark for two valid examples).

worked.ans: Sensor input, comparison by the CPU against the set value, output to switch the heating on or off, repeated continuously.
worked.q: A central heating thermostat contains an embedded system. Describe how it works. [4 marks]
steps: A temperature sensor sends the current temperature to the processor as input (1).
The CPU runs the firmware which compares it with the temperature set by the user (1).
If it is lower, the CPU sends a signal to switch the boiler/heater on, otherwise switches it off (output) (1).
This is repeated continuously in a loop so the temperature is kept near the set value (1).

worked.ans: Embedded: single fixed task, firmware in ROM, low cost and power. Laptop: many tasks, programs loaded from storage, more powerful and expensive.
worked.q: Compare an embedded system in a microwave oven with a laptop computer. [4 marks]
steps: The microwave's embedded system performs one dedicated task (controlling timer and power), whereas a laptop can run many different programs (1+1).
The embedded system's program is stored in ROM/flash as firmware and cannot be changed by the user, whereas a laptop loads programs from storage and can be updated (1).
The embedded system has a low-cost, low-power processor and small memory, while a laptop needs a powerful CPU and large RAM (1).
